notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on Ezra 4, drawn from the approved sites.

---

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records Samaritan opposition to the rebuilding work. Verses 1–5 and 24 concern the temple under Zerubbabel. Verses 6–23 form a parenthetical survey of later opposition — under Ahasuerus (Xerxes) and Artaxerxes I — directed at rebuilding the city walls (the setting of Nehemiah). The chronological range spans from Cyrus (c. 539 BC) to Artaxerxes I (464–424 BC), with verse 24 returning to the temple-work stoppage until Darius I's second year (520 BC).

**Key Insight:** The temple was completed long before the Artaxerxes episode (Ezra 6:15 places completion in 515 BC). Verses 6–23 are inserted thematically to illustrate the persistent pattern of opposition. (Enduring Word; Bible.org; Constable)

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1
**"When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the exiles were building a temple…"**

- **Enemies = Samaritans (traditional view):** Gill, Ellicott, and the Pulpit Commentary all identify these "adversaries" as the Samaritans — a mixed people descended from foreigners settled in the former Northern Kingdom by Assyrian kings (Esarhaddon and others) who intermarried with leftover Israelites. Their religion was syncretistic: "They feared the LORD, yet served their own gods" (2 Kings 17:33).
  — BibleHub (Ellicott, search excerpt); Precept Austin (citing Ryrie)

- **"Enemies" signals prior clashes:** Bob Utley (Bible.org) notes the term "enemies" suggests there had already been conflict (see Ezra 3:3, where fear of the peoples of the land is mentioned). John Walton adds that "the fact that the writer of Ezra identifies them as 'enemies' suggests … their offer of help in rebuilding the temple was not an honest one."
  — Precept Austin; Bible.org

- **"The people of the exile":** This title for the returning Jews implies that some opposition may have come not only from half-Jewish descendants but also from Jews who were never exiled but whose religious fervour and commitment differed from the returnees (Bob Utley, Bible.org).

- **Noise of the dedication ceremony:** David Guzik (Enduring Word) suggests that the celebration at the end of Ezra 3 (laying the temple foundation) alerted these scattered peoples that the returning Jews were serious about re-establishing a permanent presence.

---

### v. 2
**"Let us build with you because, like you, we seek your God…"**

- **Insincere offer:** The traditional reading across all consulted sources is that this offer was not genuine. The Pulpit Commentary says it was "a crafty endeavour … to join in the work with the intention of effectively blocking it." Ellicott notes they came "either in the spirit of hypocrites or with an intention to unite their own idolatries with the pure worship of Jehovah."
  — StudyLight.org (Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott search excerpts)

- **Political calculation:** Alexander Maclaren (cited by Enduring Word) explains: "The proposal to unite in building the Temple was a political move; for, in old-world ideas, co-operation in Temple-building was incorporation in national unity. The calculation … was that if the returning exiles could be united with the much more numerous Samaritans, they would soon be absorbed in them."

- **Syncretistic worship:** Although they claimed to "seek your God as you do," they had been sacrificing without a temple or priesthood — in violation of God's commandment. This exposed the hollowness of their claim. Bob Utley (Bible.org) notes: "The very fact that these people continued to sacrifice showed they were not in conformity to the Pentateuchal guidelines."
  — Enduring Word; Bible.org

- **Esarhaddon** reigned 681–669 BC. This Assyrian king continued the policy of deporting conquered peoples into the region. (Enduring Word; Bible.org; Constable)

---

### v. 3
**"You have no part with us in building a house for our God…"**

- **Unified refusal:** All consulted sources agree this was a righteous, necessary decision, not intolerance. The leaders (Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and heads of families) spoke with one voice. David Guzik calls it "an important step of faith to refuse a partnership that might have seemed helpful," given their lack of human and financial resources.
  — Enduring Word

- **Ellicott's defence:** "The account in 2 Kings 17 carefully studied will show that the stern refusal of the leaders was precisely in harmony with the will of God; there was nothing in it of that intolerant spirit which is sometimes imagined. The whole design of the Great Restoration would have been defeated by a concession at this point."
  — BibleHub (Ellicott, search excerpt)

- **Dr. Constable:** "Zerubbabel refused their offer because, even though they worshipped Yahweh, they did not worship Him exclusively, as the Mosaic Law specified (Exodus 20:3). Zerubbabel realized that if their commitment to God did not include a commitment to obey His revealed will, the Jewish remnant could only anticipate endless disagreement, conflict, and frustration with them."
  — StudyLight.org (Constable)

- **Appeal to Cyrus's decree:** The appeal to Cyrus's command was a "subordinate kind of justification, pleaded as subjects of the King of Persia, whose decree was absolute and exclusive" (Ellicott). It was a pragmatic as well as theological rationale.
  — BibleHub (Ellicott, search excerpt)

- **Steven Cole (Precept Austin)** applies this to modern evangelical–Catholic cooperation debates: "The danger of the appeal of these enemies was that their words were not absolute lies. They were partially true. They did worship God and sacrifice to Him. The problem was, they did not worship God alone!" He warns against mingling "the pure gospel of God's grace" with "the idols of worldly religion."

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** The refusal rested on three grounds: (1) the Samaritans had no part in true worship; (2) the Jews would build solely by themselves; (3) this was in keeping with Cyrus's command.
  — StudyLight.org (Garner-Howes)

---

### v. 4
**"Then the people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build."**

- **"Weakened the hands":** The Hebrew idiom behind "discourage" literally means "letting drop the hands" or "weakening the hands" (cf. Jeremiah 38:4). It describes loss of heart or energy.
  — BibleHub (Ezra 4:4 Commentaries); Enduring Word; Bible.org

- **True colours revealed:** All sources agree this response exposed their evil intent. As the Pulpit Commentary puts it: "Failing in their first cunning attempt, the veil of conciliation was cast off. They revealed the real hostility of spirit."
  — StudyLight.org (Pulpit Commentary)

- **"People of the land":** Before the exile, this term referred to the landed nobility. After the exile, it referred to the poorest people left in the land (2 Kings 25:12; Jeremiah 39:10). Here, Bob Utley says it seems to refer broadly to people of the Persian province "Beyond the River" (Palestine/Lebanon) — descendants of Jews and pagans with a partial knowledge of YHWH.
  — Bible.org

---

### v. 5
**"They hired counselors against them to frustrate their plans throughout the reign of Cyrus … down to the reign of Darius."**

- **Sustained political opposition:** This involved paid lobbyists or bribed officials at the Persian court who worked to undermine the Jewish leadership over many years (c. 536–520 BC). Constable notes: "Bribery as a practice was well known in Persian times."
  — StudyLight.org (Constable); Enduring Word

- **Steven Cole (Precept Austin):** "Whether these hired counselors operated at the royal court or whether they circulated among the Jews, or both, they spread half-truths and misinformation to undermine the leadership of Zerubbabel and Jeshua."

- **Time span:** Bob Utley notes the time element poses a difficulty — was this opposition continuous from Sheshbazzar's day into Zerubbabel's? Some argue Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel may be the same person; others see a gap.
  — Bible.org

---

### v. 6
**"At the beginning of the reign of Xerxes, an accusation was lodged…"**

- **Chronological jump:** This verse moves forward perhaps 50 years to the reign of Ahasuerus/Xerxes I (486–464 BC), the king of Esther. The temple was long finished. The accusation concerned something else — likely the city and its walls.
  — Enduring Word; Bible.org; Constable

- **Nothing came of it:** Derek Kidner (cited in Enduring Word) says: "The mention of him here marks simply the passage of time, which had still not cooled the enemy's antagonism. But evidently nothing came of this attempt."

- **Pattern of opposition:** Ezra includes this brief notice to demonstrate the unrelenting nature of Samaritan hostility across decades and multiple reigns.
  — Constable; Precept Austin

---

### vv. 7–8
**"In the days of Artaxerxes … Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel … wrote a letter … written in Aramaic and then translated. Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote the letter…"**

- **Artaxerxes I (464–424 BC):** This is the king under whom both Ezra (Ezra 7–10) and Nehemiah served. He is not to be confused with the pseudo-Smerdis (also called Artaxerxes by some older commentators like Ellicott). The letter concerns rebuilding the city walls, not the temple — a point made emphatically by Kidner, Guzik, Constable, and Utley.
  — Enduring Word; Constable; Bible.org

- **Aramaic section begins (4:8–6:18):** From here through Ezra 6:18, the text is in Aramaic, the diplomatic language of the Persian Empire. Guzik notes: "The letter was probably dictated in Persian to a scribe, who translated it into Aramaic and wrote it down in Aramaic script."
  — Enduring Word; Bible.org

- **"Rehum the commander":** The highest-ranking Persian official in Samaria who dictated the letter. "Shimshai the scribe": Each Persian satrap had a special scribe appointed by the king to keep tabs on him (Herodotus, Hist. 3.128, cited in Bible.org).
  — Bible.org

- **Older view (Ellicott):** Ellicott thought this Artaxerxes might be Gomates (the Magian priest who impersonated Smerdis, reigning only seven months), partly because "days" not "reign" is used. However, most modern commentators reject this, noting the reference to "walls" in v. 12 fits Nehemiah's era.
  — BibleHub (Ellicott, search excerpt)

---

### vv. 9–10
**"From Rehum … Shimshai … the judges and officials over Tripolis, Persia, Erech and Babylon, the Elamites of Susa, and the rest of the peoples whom … Ashurbanipal deported…"**

- **Coalition of peoples:** The letter-writers list many ethnic groups to give the impression that everyone agrees against the Jews. Steven Cole calls this a tactic: "The ploy behind such tactics is to imply, 'Everyone is against these people.'"
  — Precept Austin

- **Ashurbanipal (Osnappar):** Son of Esarhaddon, the last great Assyrian king (669–c. 627 BC), who continued deportations into Samaria. Constable notes that this may refer specifically to the deportation of Susa in 645 BC.
  — Constable; Bible.org

- **"West of the Euphrates" (Beyond the River):** The Persian administrative province encompassing Syria and Palestine.
  — Constable

---

### vv. 11–12
**"The Jews … are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city, restoring its walls, and repairing its foundations."**

- **City walls, not the temple:** This is the critical exegetical point. The temple was completed by 515 BC; Artaxerxes I reigned 464–424 BC. Kidner: "It should hardly need emphasising that the walls and foundations are those of the city, not the Temple; but the two operations are often confused. By the reign of Artaxerxes the new Temple had been standing for half a century."
  — Enduring Word

- **The accusation:** The Samaritans characterise Jerusalem as "rebellious and wicked" based on its pre-exilic history (Hezekiah's withholding tribute, Zedekiah's revolt against Babylon). This was a clever mixture of truth and lies — the past was true, but the present builders had no rebellious intent.
  — Enduring Word; Constable

---

### v. 13
**"If that city is rebuilt … they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer."**

- **Financial appeal:** The letter appeals to the king's financial interest — the surest way to get a Persian monarch's attention. This was a false accusation: the returned exiles were not a rebellious faction.
  — Enduring Word; Precept Austin; Constable

- **Three threatened consequences:** Bob Utley summarises: (1) loss of tax revenue; (2) loss of face (reputation); (3) loss of land (the Jews once controlled Palestine and might try again).
  — Bible.org

---

### v. 14
**"Because we are in the service of the palace…"**

- **"We eat the salt of the palace":** The literal Aramaic phrase. Adam Clarke (cited in Enduring Word) explains: "We live on the king's bounty, and must be faithful to our benefactor." Yamauchi notes that the English word "salary" derives from the Latin *salarium*, the ration of salt given to soldiers. The phrase expresses loyalty and obligation.
  — Enduring Word; Precept Austin; Bible.org

---

### vv. 15–16
**"Search the record books … this city is a rebellious city … you will have no dominion west of the Euphrates."**

- **Appeal to historical records:** The Samaritans knew that Persian archives contained Babylonian and Assyrian records documenting Jerusalem's revolts. McConville (cited in Constable) lists Hezekiah's withholding of tribute (2 Kings 18:7) and Zedekiah's rebellion (2 Kings 24:20ff.) as likely examples.
  — Constable

- **Exaggerated threat:** The claim that Persia would lose all territory west of the Euphrates was a wild overstatement given the tiny Jewish population.
  — Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary (search excerpt); Enduring Word

---

### vv. 17–22
**"Then the king sent this reply … I issued a decree, and a search was conducted … Now, therefore, issue an order for these men to stop…"**

- **The king's research confirmed the accusation:** Artaxerxes found that Jerusalem did have a history of revolt. He focused on the truthful part of the Samaritans' letter.
  — Enduring Word

- **"Mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem":** Clarke notes this refers to David and Solomon, whose dominion extended to the Euphrates (2 Samuel 8:3ff.; 1 Kings 4:21). In Artaxerxes' mind, this meant Judah had the potential to return to its powerful past.
  — Enduring Word (citing Clarke)

- **"Until I so order" (v. 21):** A providential loophole. The decree was temporary — "until a decree is issued by me." About two years later (444 BC), Artaxerxes released Nehemiah to rebuild the walls (Nehemiah 2:8). Constable suggests the king concluded that, all things considered, it was better to have Jerusalem defended than undefended.
  — Enduring Word; Constable; Precept Austin

- **Bob Utley (Bible.org) notes the irony:** Artaxerxes is the very king who later allowed Ezra to return and responded positively to Nehemiah's request to rebuild the walls.

---

### v. 23
**"They went immediately to the Jews in Jerusalem and forcibly stopped them."**

- **"By force of arms":** The Samaritans acted "in haste" — not merely out of obedience but from eagerness to crush the work. Gill says they went "not only in obedience to the king's command, but from an eagerness of spirit to put a stop to the proceedings of the Jews, to whom they had an aversion."
  — BibleHub (Gill, search excerpt)

- **Possible destruction of work:** From Nehemiah 1:3, it seems the Samaritans may not only have stopped the work but also destroyed what had been built and burned the gates.
  — Constable; Bible.org

- **Fensham (cited in Constable):** "This was a day of great shame to the Jewish population because their honest endeavour was thwarted by their archenemies, the Samaritans, and it was forced on them by Samaritan soldiers."

---

### v. 24
**"Thus the construction of the house of God in Jerusalem ceased, and it remained at a standstill until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia."**

- **Return to the temple narrative:** This verse picks up the thread from verse 5 after the long parenthesis of verses 6–23. Kidner: "The word 'Thus' would at first point us to the verse immediately before this; but it only makes sense if it is picking up the thread of verse 5 which was dropped for the long parenthesis (verses 6-23). The time is again that of Zerubbabel."
  — Enduring Word

- **Duration of stoppage:** The work on the temple ceased for roughly 15–16 years — from Cyrus's reign until the second year of Darius I Hystaspes (520 BC, when Haggai and Zechariah began prophesying, Ezra 5:1).
  — Enduring Word; Precept Austin; Constable

- **Darius I (not Darius the Mede):** Gill is emphatic that this is Darius Hystaspis (522–486 BC), not Darius Nothus or the Darius of Daniel. The chronology from Cyrus to the sixth year of Darius (when the temple was finished, Ezra 6:15) covers about 21 years, making the age of Zerubbabel and eyewitnesses of Solomon's temple plausible.
  — BibleHub (Gill, search excerpt)

- **Altar worship continued:** Ellicott notes: "The suspension of the general enterprise … lasted nearly two years. But it must be remembered that the altar was still the centre of a certain amount of worship."
  — BibleHub (Ellicott, search excerpt)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The consulted sources show remarkably little doctrinal disagreement on Ezra 4 across Protestant traditions. The broad consensus is that Zerubbabel's refusal was righteous and necessary. However, some differences in emphasis emerge:

### Reformed / Presbyterian
No distinctively Reformed commentary was found in the search results for Ezra 4. The traditional Reformed approach would likely stress God's sovereign preservation of His covenant people through political opposition, consistent with the emphasis of sources like the Gospel Coalition and Ligonier on God's providence in redemptive history.

### Baptist
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** emphasises spiritual warfare: "It is the constant purpose of Satan to bring the work of God's people to a halt (2 Timothy 4:14-15)." Five lessons are drawn: (1) triumph in one matter doesn't prevent attack elsewhere; (2) false religionists can appear innocent; (3) the Devil always has prominent persons ready to do his bidding; (4) past mistakes hinder future testimony; (5) it is easy for God's work to be stopped.
  — StudyLight.org (Garner-Howes, search excerpt)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)** reads the opposition through a spiritual-warfare lens, comparing the Samaritan letter's mixture of truth and lies to Satan's accusations against believers (Revelation 12:10). He emphasises that the enemy's "only victory was to delay the work, not to defeat it" — a note of charismatic encouragement that God's purposes cannot ultimately be stopped.
  — Enduring Word

### Methodist / Wesleyan / Holiness
- **Steven Cole (Precept Austin)** emphasises personal application for the believer's spiritual life: "Whenever you make a commitment to the Lord, be prepared to face the enemy's unrelenting attempt to set you back." He warns against four wrong responses: giving up, settling for second best, blaming leaders, and spiritualising laziness as "God's timing." He also explicitly applies vv. 1–3 to warn against evangelical compromise with Roman Catholicism.
  — Precept Austin

### Lutheran
No Lutheran-specific commentary on Ezra 4 was found in the search results from LCMS.org or 1517.org.

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship / NET Bible
- The **NET Bible** notes translation choices such as "you have no right" (v. 3) rather than "you have nothing in common," and "threat of armed force" (v. 23). The NET also preserves the Aramaic section notation and notes that Ashurbanipal (v. 10) is the "great and honorable" Assyrian king who deported peoples into Samaria.
  — netbible.org

- **Dr. Constable** cites R.J. Coggins (JTS, 1965) who argues that "'people of the land' is a vague term being attached to different groups during different phases … Chronologically, it cannot refer to Samaritan opposition, since the Samaritan sect is a much later emergence." This scholarly caution is not adopted by most of the devotional/commentary sources.
  — StudyLight.org (Constable)

### Catholic / Orthodox
No Catholic or Orthodox commentary on Ezra 4 was available from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org in the search results.

---

## Summary of Key Themes Across Sources

1. **Discernment in partnerships:** All sources agree Zerubbabel's refusal was righteous — syncretistic worship cannot be yoked with pure worship of Yahweh.

2. **The parenthetical structure:** Verses 6–23 are a thematic, not chronological, insertion illustrating persistent opposition across generations. Verse 24 returns to the temple narrative of verses 1–5.

3. **Temple vs. city walls:** The letter to Artaxerxes concerns city walls (Nehemiah's era), not the temple (already completed). Confusing the two leads to chronological errors.

4. **Satanic opposition:** Nearly all sources frame the chapter as a case study in spiritual warfare — the enemy uses compromise, discouragement, fear, false accusation, political pressure, and force.

5. **God's purposes prevail:** The work was delayed, not defeated. The decree contained a providential loophole ("until I so order"), and under Darius the temple was finished (Ezra 6:15).
